memoryText: For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Jeremiah 2:13 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
God diagnoses the whole human problem in one verse, and he calls it two evils.

The first evil is leaving the fountain. God describes himself as “the fountain of living waters.” In a dry land, a spring of living water is life. It does not run out or need to be dug. It simply flows. Every good thing we need comes from him, and he offers it freely. To forsake him is to walk away from the one source that cannot fail.

The second evil is building our own cisterns. A cistern is a hole cut in rock to collect rainwater. It is man-made, limited, and dependent on circumstances. And these are “broken” cisterns, cracked, so they cannot even hold what they collect. The picture is of tremendous effort invested in something that cannot deliver. We chisel away at success, approval, comfort, and control, and each time the water drains out.

What stands out is the tone. God is not only angry. He is astonished. Earlier in the chapter he says, “Be appalled, O heavens, at this.” It is baffling to him that anyone would trade a spring for a leaky tank. And behind the astonishment is grief. He loves his people and wants them to have what satisfies.

Jesus claimed to be this fountain. “Let the one who is thirsty come.” The remedy for broken cisterns is not trying harder but turning back. Say this verse when you feel empty, and ask what cistern you have been drinking from.
weekInReview: This week you began the exile unit by reading the last days of the kingdom of Judah. You saw Manasseh’s evil, Josiah’s tender-hearted reform, and the sobering line that the LORD still did not turn from his anger. You read the account of Jerusalem’s fall in 2 Kings, with the small candle of Jehoiachin’s release at the end. You prayed Psalm 89’s painful second half and the grief of Psalm 137, learning that honest prayer includes lament. And you met Jeremiah, called before he was born, who named the two evils of his people: forsaking the fountain of living waters and digging broken cisterns. His early preaching called them to return and to circumcise their hearts. The week taught that outward reform is not enough, that God invites us to return, and that he is the only source of life.
reflectionQuestions: Josiah found the Book of the Law and tore his clothes. How do you respond when God’s word exposes something in your life?
Jeremiah describes forsaking the fountain and digging broken cisterns. What is one cistern you tend to drink from instead of God?
Jesus calls himself the source of living water (John 7:37-38). What would it look like to come to him as thirsty this week?
prayerPrompts: Confess the cisterns you have dug.
Thank Jesus for giving water that satisfies.
